newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banker says Holocaust fund hunt continues.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banker says Holocaust fund hunt continues.

text.p: Swiss bankers and world Jewish groups will continue working together to track lost Holocaust accounts despite lingering tension over a Swiss minister's claim of Jewish "blackmail", an influential banker said on Wednesday.

Hans Baer, member of a commission set up by the banks and Jewish groups to track down dormant accounts in Swiss banks, said its work continued even after Berne on Tuesday ignored demands for an apology for the blackmail remark.
"The work of the commission is not affected," Baer, vice-chairman of the Swiss Bankers Association and the country's most prominent Jewish banker, told Reuters.

The commission's future was called into question by the head of Israel's Jewish Agency on Tuesday after the Swiss government ignored demands it denounce remarks by Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz.

Avraham Burg, also a member of the commission, said he would not take part in its search for dormant accounts in Swiss banks left by Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust unless the Swiss members condemned Delamuraz's remarks.
Delamuraz stirred angry protest by describing as "blackmail" Jewish demands for quick compensation for Holocaust victims and their heirs.

The Federal Council, or cabinet, on Tuesday said it was not apologising because Delamuraz had been misunderstood and reactions were excessive -- an apparent reference to threats by Jewish groups headed by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) to call a boycott against Swiss banks.
But Baer said the commission, headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker, was working in the interest of the Jewish Agency and WJC, who set it up last May with Swiss banks.
"I would not understand this (a Jewish Agency withdrawal). The auditors are working in the interest of the Jewish groups," Baer said.

The Volcker commission, which has three members appointed by Jewish groups and three by the Swiss Bankers Association as well as two alternates from each side, launched operations in November by naming three big international accounting firms to audit records at Swiss banks.
The commission will use the audits as its basis for reporting in mid-1998 on the extent of dormant accounts left in banks in neutral war-time Switzerland by Jews and other victims of the Nazis.

"The auditors are doing the actual work now and the work is continuing. The commission itself has a supervisory role at the moment and only meets three or four times a year," Baer said, adding the next meeting would be January 31.
Baer said the three Swiss members and two alternates had not been contacted directly yet by Burg, who appealed in a Jerusalem statement on Tuesday for them to denounce Delamuraz's comments.
Baer said the Swiss commission members would consider an answer after all five return from New Year holidays next week and only at Burg's direct request.
"The Swiss delegation has heard nothing directly from Burg and we cannot talk with him through the newspapers," Baer said.

Separately, Bernard Lavrie, spokesman for the Jewish community in French-speaking Switzerland, told the newspaper Tribune de Geneve the government's statement on Tuesday amounted to a clear expression of regret at the Delamuraz remarks.
"This ought to be enough for the WJC, and it should not demand an official apology under the seal of the (Swiss) Confederation," he said.
"But I think we will return to calmer waters. Who has any interest in reigniting this quarrel? After all, it should be remembered that it is the money that is being sought."
